description:
I'm Ahmad Kura , a computer science graduate and AI engineer, leading Team Pandas. I want to build AI software with NASA data that actually works by the end of the weekend, with a focus on astronaut health on long missions.

Looking for: web developers, data analysts/visualizers, designers and storytellers for the demo, and anyone into health or human space exploration.

No need to be an expert. If you're curious, reliable and ready to build, join Team Pandas.
summary: VIGIL is a crew health console for astronauts who are not physicians, built for missions where Earth is too far away to ask in time. On the way to Mars a message takes up to about 22 minutes to reach Earth, so a crew must judge its own health first. VIGIL answers three questions: What is my status? Why does it matter here? What do I do now? It rates each vital sign against a threshold with a cited source, links readings to body systems and to NASA’s named spaceflight risks, and adjusts priorities and radiation estimates to the environment the crew is in. When something needs attention, it opens a guided protocol that works without Earth and records every step. Before the next contact window, it packs the crew’s status into a short plain-text brief for flight surgeons. VIGIL works fully offline after one visit, needs no server or account, and uses simulated data. It is a concept demonstration, not a medical device.
details:
What it does

VIGIL is a health console for a four-person crew on a Mars mission. It helps astronauts who are not physicians look after themselves and each other when Earth is minutes away. It answers three questions.

What is my status?

The Overview shows the latest reading of each vital sign (heart rate, blood pressure, heart rate variability, core temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood, cognitive readiness, blood oxygen and a daily vision self-check). Each reading is rated nominal, watch or action. Every rating uses a colour, an icon and a word, and every threshold shows where it comes from. A crew bar and "Crew at a glance" cards show who needs attention, and the app offers light and dark themes for different lighting conditions.

Why does it matter here?

The Body Map groups readings into eight body systems and links each one to the NASA Human Research Program risks that affect it. The crew can switch between four environments (spacecraft transit, orbital station, pressurized rover and Mars surface base). The environment changes the signal delay to Earth, the ranking of the five spaceflight hazards, and the radiation dose rate. The radiation panel shows career dose against NASA's 600 mSv limit and how many days are left at today's rate.

What do I do now?

The Triage page lists every watch or action reading, most urgent first. Each alert opens a guided protocol in four parts: confirm the reading, check for red-flag symptoms, take low-risk self-care steps, and escalate. Each step is timestamped and saved, so a protocol can be resumed. If Earth is less than a second away, VIGIL tells the crew to consult the flight surgeon now. On the Mars mission it tells them to complete the first steps without waiting, then send a brief. The Downlink page builds that brief as a few kilobytes of plain text.

A Routine page supports prevention with a daily checklist (exercise, sleep, nutrition, check-ins, a vision check), points and streaks. Exercise adherence feeds the rating for bones and muscles.

How it works

VIGIL is a single-page web app. All processing happens in the browser, with no server or account. After the first visit VIGIL is stored on the device as an installable app, so every page, protocol and the Downlink brief work with no network connection. Thresholds are stored as data, each value with its unit and source, and a set of tested functions turns readings into ratings, alerts, protocol state and the brief. Where published figures leave a gap, the rule is labelled as a team rule and is not presented as clinical fact. Protocols never name medicines or doses.

The demo uses a seeded simulation of 30 mission days with two storylines: the flight engineer builds up sleep debt from day 22, and the mission specialist develops a 38.3 °C fever on day 29. A guided tour walks a new visitor through the fever case, from alert to downlink, in about a minute.

What makes it creative

  • Distance from Earth is a design input. The same reading leads to different guidance depending on how long a reply from Earth would take.
  • It keeps working with no connection to Earth. After one visit, every page and protocol runs on the device.
  • The Body Map explains why a number matters, by linking it to NASA's named spaceflight risks, not just whether it is high or low.
  • It is honest by design. Every threshold shows its source, and the rules we made ourselves are labelled.

Factors we considered

  • The users are not physicians, so we used plain language and step-by-step checks.
  • Status never relies on colour alone. Icons and words make it readable for everyone.
  • Safety comes first. No medicines or doses are named, and any red-flag symptom escalates straight away.
  • A deep-space crew cannot depend on servers on Earth, so VIGIL works fully offline and all processing happens on the device.

Benefits

  • The crew can act on a health concern straight away instead of waiting up to 45 minutes for a reply from Earth.
  • Every number is traceable to its source, which helps the crew and the ground trust and check it.
  • The brief gives flight surgeons a short, timestamped record of what was measured and what was done.
  • Routine and streaks encourage the daily habits that help the body cope with long missions.

What we hope to achieve

We want to show that an Earth-independent health tool can be clear, honest about its limits, and grounded in NASA data. Next steps would be input from real wearables and medical devices, native tablet packaging, and review of every rule and protocol by flight surgeons.

Tools, languages and software

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Motion, Zustand, React Router, Recharts, vite-plugin-pwa (offline support), lucide-react icons, IBM Plex fonts, Vitest, oxlint and Playwright (for browser tests, screenshots and the deck PDF). Hosted on Vercel, with the code on GitHub. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant to help plan the build, research sources and write the code; the team directed the work and reviewed it at each stage.
